content.text: A ref is a plain, mutable box that React hands back unchanged on every render and never watches. That makes it right for values the screen doesn't show, like timer ids, DOM nodes and non-React objects, and wrong for anything the JSX displays. Reading or writing
during render also breaks purity: do it in event handlers and Effects.

A performance review flags the post composer: it re-renders on every keystroke. The fix looks clever: move the text from state into a ref, so typing no longer renders anything. It ships, and the bug reports follow. The "0/280" counter never moves, and the Post button stays disabled however much you type. Then a notification arrives, something unrelated re-renders the composer, and the counter suddenly jumps to "143/280". React wasn't broken. The component was showing a value React had no idea existed.
without the re-render. It's a cheaper box for any value: write to it whenever you like, read it in JSX, and save renders along the way.

There's a lot of truth in it, which is why it sticks. A ref does persist across renders like state, and changing it doesn't re-render, which is exactly how React's docs introduce refs: a way to remember information without triggering new renders. The docs even note that
could in principle be built on top of

. And "avoid unnecessary re-renders" is advice every React developer hears early. What the belief leaves out is the other half: React never looks at a ref, so nothing that depends on it updates by itself, and touching it during render makes the component impure.
A ref is a box React hands back and never watches
, and on every later render it returns that same object. You can change

at any time, and the change is visible immediately, with no snapshot and no queue. React doesn't know when that happens, so it schedules nothing. That's the whole feature, and it's why React's docs call
: they let you step outside React's data flow, which is useful exactly when the value has nothing to do with what's on screen.
Rendering from a ref shows a stale value

captures whatever the ref held when the component last rendered for some other reason. Typing changes the ref but triggers no render, so the counter keeps its old value until an unrelated state change happens to re-render the composer. The rule from React's docs is simple: if a value is used for rendering, keep it in state.

content.text: If re-rendering on every keystroke is a real, measured problem, the fix is to keep the text in the smallest component that shows it, not to hide it from React. Re-rendering a textarea, a counter and a button is cheap.
Reading or writing during render is a side effect
The other half of the rule is about the component body. Patterns like
at the top level of a component write to a ref during render. React expects render to be a

: it may call your component twice in Strict Mode, or start a render and throw it away. A ref write from a render that never reached the screen still happened, so the ref ends up describing renders the user never saw. Reading during render is just as unreliable: a DOM ref is still

on the first render, because React only sets it during the commit. React's docs warn that such a component might still work, but most of the newer features React is adding rely on render staying pure.

blocks.title: Don't let a ref fight React over the DOM

content.text: A DOM ref is for focusing, scrolling, measuring and calling browser APIs. Removing nodes from, or adding children to, elements React renders leaves React with a DOM it doesn't expect, and React's docs show this crashing on the next update. Only change parts of the DOM that React has no reason to update.

React's docs list a short set of jobs: storing timeout and interval ids, holding DOM nodes, and keeping other objects that aren't needed to calculate the JSX, like an instance of a third-party player or map. All of them are read and written in event handlers and Effects, never during render:
The query appears in the input, so it's state. The timer id never appears anywhere; only the next keystroke needs it, to cancel the pending search, so it's a ref.

content.text: Use them to focus, scroll, measure and drive third-party widgets, and leave adding and removing elements to React.
